before: Conditional rendering means choosing which JSX belongs in this render. The expression condition ? yes : no chooses one branch. Here false selects null, which adds no panel to the tree; it is not merely invisible CSS.

React.useState(false) supplies the current Boolean and its setter. The click callback runs after a click, not while rendering. setOpen(value => !value) queues the opposite Boolean from pending state. Keep the Hook at the component’s top level, before any conditional return. aria-expanded mirrors the same value; aria-controls names the panel ID.

Optional practice: Replace the paragraph text, then explain why null does not create an empty section. The checks cover these finite behaviors; a matching DOM alone does not prove every implementation choice. The frame supplies React and mounts App. No imports, server, persistence or network are involved.
after: Conditional rendering means choosing what React shows. `condition ? yes : no` chooses one of two results. Here, `null` means there is no panel to show.
The `open` state is either true or false. Each click changes it to the opposite value. `aria-expanded` tells assistive tools whether the panel is open. It uses that same state value.

Starting with `useState(true)` would show the panel immediately. `aria-controls="detail"` connects the button to the panel's matching ID. Keep `useState` at the top of the component so it runs in the same order each time.
Make `Details` add and remove the section. Keep `aria-expanded` correct for both states. Returning `null` removes the panel; it does not leave an empty section behind.

Closed
